nameStory: This cricket gets its name from two key traits: it's originally from Japan (though now found throughout eastern North America), and it spends much of its life underground in burrows it digs in the soil. Unlike many crickets that live above ground on plants or surfaces, this species is a true earth-dweller that excavates its own cozy underground hideouts.
description: The Japanese Burrowing Cricket is a small, brownish cricket that lives most of its life underground in self-made burrows. These sturdy little insects are about the size of a house cricket, with strong digging legs and a robust build perfect for their subterranean lifestyle. They're actually non-native visitors from Asia that arrived in the U.S. in 1959, likely as eggs hidden in the soil of imported plants. Despite being introduced species, they're considered quite harmless and non-destructive to gardens and crops.

idTips.label: Burrowing behavior
idTips.description: Look for small, round holes in soft soil about the width of a pencil - these are their burrow entrances, often with a tiny mound of excavated dirt nearby

idTips.label: Body build
idTips.description: Stocky, robust cricket with noticeably strong, thick hind legs built for digging rather than the long, thin jumping legs of surface crickets

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Mottled brown to dark brown coloring that feels rough to the touch, helping them blend with soil and earth

idTips.label: Underground chirping
idTips.description: Males produce a softer, more muffled chirping sound that seems to come from below ground rather than from plants or surfaces

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Compact cricket roughly the length of your thumbnail, with a somewhat flattened appearance and shorter antennae than typical house crickets

habitat: Japanese Burrowing Crickets prefer areas with loose, well-draining soil where they can easily excavate their burrows. You'll find them in gardens, park lawns, sandy areas near trails, and the soft earth around building foundations. They particularly favor spots with some moisture but good drainage, avoiding both waterlogged areas and completely dry, compacted soils.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from overwintering burrows and begin singing to attract mates. Look and listen for their muffled chirping coming from small holes in warming soil.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with most obvious signs - fresh burrow holes, active digging, and regular evening chirping from underground. Young crickets are developing in deeper burrows.
seasonality.fall: Adults are still active but beginning to prepare winter burrows. Chirping becomes less frequent as temperatures drop and they focus on survival preparations.
seasonality.winter: Crickets overwinter as eggs or young nymphs deep in their burrows, invisible to casual observation. Burrow entrances may be sealed or collapsed.

funFact: These crickets are such dedicated engineers that they construct different types of burrows for different purposes - shallow ones for daily hiding and deeper, more elaborate ones for overwintering that can extend nearly a foot underground with multiple chambers!
confusionNotes: Most people assume any chirping cricket lives above ground, so the underground singing can be puzzling. If you hear cricket sounds but can't see any crickets on plants or surfaces, look down at the soil for small holes - you've probably found Japanese Burrowing Crickets. Memory trick: "Hear but can't see? Look at your feet!"
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'invasive,' these crickets are remarkably well-behaved immigrants that don't damage plants or compete aggressively with native species. Their spread northward through New England represents a quiet, gradual expansion rather than a dramatic ecological disruption, making them one of the more benign non-native species in our region.
compareHints: Since this is the only Velarifictorus species in New England, compare it to common field crickets and house crickets. Japanese Burrowing Crickets are much more robust and stocky than the slender field crickets you see hopping in grass, and they lack the long, delicate antennae of house crickets. Most importantly, if you find a cricket actually in a burrow or emerging from soil, it's almost certainly this species rather than any native cricket.
